paras: The lynching of an unnamed Black man at Grand Forks, Dakota, was a mob killing reported only in a June 1888 editorial in the Western Appeal of St. Paul, Minnesota, which dated it to "only a short time ago." According to the editorial, the man was accused of raping a white woman, pursued into Minnesota by a mob, taken back to Grand Forks and torn apart by teams of horses. The paper cited the case as proof that lynching for alleged rape reached "even up here, in the free Northwest," and said the woman later admitted he had not raped her.
The editorial gave no name, date or other particulars for the case. It said only that "a Colored man was accused of raping a white woman in Grand Forks, Dakota."

The accused man escaped and crossed into Minnesota, where he was overtaken by a mob that had followed him. The mob took him from Minnesota back to Grand Forks. There, in the editorial's words, "a team of horses was attached to his arms and another to his feet and he was literally drawn asunder."

The Western Appeal wrote that the woman afterward "confessed that he did not" rape her, but said she had thought he meant to when she gave the alarm. The editorial added that "Nothing was ever done in vindication," and no report of an inquest, arrest or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Grand Forks killing survives in the coverage only as a passing example in an editorial on June 9, 1888, whose main subject was the confession of Richard Carney, a man under sentence of death in New Jersey. Carney had confessed to the assault for which Samuel Johnson, known as Mingo Jack, had been lynched two years earlier, and the Western Appeal set the Grand Forks case beside it as a second lynching on a false accusation. The paper condemned what it called "that same fiendish prejudice" of white men toward Black men accused by white women and ended with the demand "Lynch law must go."

bases: A1 describes a mob pursuing an accused Black man into Minnesota, taking him back to Grand Forks and killing him by tearing him apart with horses.

A1 says a 'mob' seized a man accused of raping a white woman and killed him without any legal process, which fits the definition, but it is a single retrospective editorial with no name, date, size of the mob or named source.
The only account is a passing reference in one St. Paul editorial (A1); no first report, local coverage or follow-up was found.
